stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the agronomists' conclusion?
stimulus:
Winter cover crops such as cereal rye are planted after harvest and killed in spring, which leaves a layer of residue on the soil surface. That residue slows evaporation, so the soil under it holds more water into midsummer, when corn is most sensitive to moisture stress. Agronomists at a Nebraska research farm compared corn grown after rye with corn grown on bare soil over eight seasons, four wet and four dry. They concluded that a rye cover crop raises corn yields in dry seasons, when the extra stored water matters most.

Average Corn Yield (bushels per acre)
Season type | Bare soil | After rye
Wet | 182 | 176
Dry | 131 | 154
choices: In wet seasons, corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre, while corn grown after rye yielded 176.
Corn grown on bare soil yielded 182 bushels per acre in wet seasons but only 131 bushels per acre in dry seasons.
In dry seasons, corn grown after rye yielded 154 bushels per acre, while corn grown on bare soil yielded 131.
Corn grown after rye yielded more per acre than corn grown on bare soil in both wet seasons and dry seasons.
explanation: The conclusion is limited to dry seasons and compares rye with bare soil. So you need the dry row, with rye higher than bare soil. Choice C gives exactly that: 154 bushels against 131.

A.why: You ignored the condition the claim depends on. The conclusion is about dry seasons, and this choice reports only the wet row. In that row rye doesn't even raise yields.

B.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice holds the treatment fixed at bare soil and compares weather conditions. That shows drought lowers yield, not that rye raises it.

D.why: You misread the wet row. In wet seasons corn after rye yielded 176 bushels, less than the 182 bushels on bare soil.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Recognize that rye's benefit is visible only in dry seasons; one data point directly shows it.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the team's hypothesis?
stimulus:
When seismic waves pass from hard bedrock into the soft sediments that fill many valleys, they slow down and grow in amplitude, so the ground shakes harder. Seismologists express this as an amplification factor: peak shaking at a sediment site divided by peak shaking at a nearby bedrock site. Distant earthquakes arrive dominated by long-period waves, which sediment layers tend to resonate with. For that reason, one team hypothesized that basin sediments amplify shaking from distant earthquakes more than shaking from nearby ones.

Average Peak Ground Acceleration (cm/s²)
Earthquake distance | Bedrock sites | Sediment sites
Under 50 km | 120 | 180
Over 150 km | 20 | 50
choices: For nearby earthquakes, sediment sites exceeded bedrock sites by 60 cm/s², whereas for distant ones the gap was only 30 cm/s².
Sediment sites recorded stronger shaking than bedrock sites did for both nearby earthquakes and distant earthquakes.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for nearby earthquakes but 1.5 times for distant ones.
Shaking at sediment sites was 2.5 times that at bedrock sites for distant earthquakes but 1.5 times for nearby ones.
explanation: The passage defines amplification as a ratio, sediment divided by bedrock. So you have to compute it: 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5 for distant earthquakes and 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5 for nearby ones. Choice D shows that distant earthquakes are amplified more, which is what the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You used raw differences when the passage defined amplification as a ratio. The gaps are accurate, but subtraction doesn't measure the amplification factor. Measured as a ratio, the result goes the other way.

B.why: You chose a true statement that supports a broader claim, that sediments amplify shaking at all. The hypothesis is about which distance is amplified more, and this choice doesn't compare the two.

C.why: You reversed the ratios. Nearby earthquakes give 180 ÷ 120 = 1.5, and distant ones give 50 ÷ 20 = 2.5, not the other way around.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Calculate amplification factors (ratios, not absolute gaps); recognize 2.5× > 1.5× and avoid reversed distractor.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken Wierzbicki's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Hillshading simulates the shadows that terrain casts under light from one direction. It is often added to contour maps to make relief easier to see. Cartographer Tomasz Wierzbicki asked novice and experienced map readers to identify the easiest walking routes on contour-only or hillshaded versions of the same maps. Experienced readers can already picture terrain from contour lines alone. Wierzbicki therefore hypothesized that hillshading would improve novices' accuracy more than it would improve experienced readers' accuracy.

Route Choices Judged Correct (%)
Reader group | Contour-only map | Hillshaded map
Novice | 58 | 64
Experienced | 71 | 83
choices: Hillshading raised experienced readers' accuracy by 12 percentage points but raised novices' accuracy by only 6 points.
Novices chose correct routes 64% of the time with hillshaded maps and 58% of the time with contour-only maps.
Experienced readers chose correct routes more often than novices did with both contour-only and hillshaded maps.
Hillshading raised novices' accuracy by 12 percentage points but raised experienced readers' accuracy by only 6 points.
explanation: The hypothesis predicts that the novices' gain from hillshading will be larger than the experienced readers' gain. To weaken it, you need the opposite. Experienced readers gained 12 points (71 to 83), and novices gained only 6 (58 to 64). Choice A states that.

B.why: You stopped at one group. This choice shows that novices improved, but the hypothesis compares the size of the improvement across both groups. A single row can't weaken that comparison.

C.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice compares reader groups within each map type. The hypothesis is about how much hillshading changes each group's accuracy.

D.why: You swapped the rows. Novices gained 6 points and experienced readers gained 12. Also, the reversed version would support the hypothesis, not weaken it.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Calculate gains for both groups (6 vs 12 points); recognize that experienced gaining more weakens the hypothesis.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the analysts' conclusion?
stimulus:
Economists who study employee turnover often find that workers leave jobs when their schedules clash with obligations outside work. A logistics firm let some of its office staff work remotely while others remained on-site. Analysts tracked who quit over the following year and separated employees who reported caring for a child or relative from those who did not. The analysts concluded that remote eligibility lowers quit rates among caregivers but has little effect on employees without caregiving duties.

Annual Quit Rate (%)
Employee group | On-site | Remote-eligible
Caregivers | 18 | 9
Non-caregivers | 11 | 10
choices: Remote-eligible caregivers quit at a rate of 9%, half the 18% rate among caregivers who remained on-site.
Among on-site employees, caregivers quit at a rate of 18%, while non-caregivers quit at a rate of 11%.
Remote-eligible non-caregivers quit at a rate of 10%, well below the 18% rate among on-site non-caregivers.
Remote eligibility cut caregivers' quit rate from 18% to 9% but changed non-caregivers' rate only from 11% to 10%.
explanation: The conclusion has two parts: a large drop for caregivers and little change for non-caregivers. Choice D covers both. Caregivers' quit rate fell from 18% to 9%, and non-caregivers' barely moved, from 11% to 10%.

A.why: You supported only half of the conclusion. This choice shows the drop for caregivers but says nothing about the claim that remote work has little effect on non-caregivers.

B.why: You compared the wrong cells. This choice holds work arrangement fixed at on-site and compares the two employee groups, so it doesn't show any effect of remote eligibility.

C.why: You read across into the wrong row. On-site non-caregivers quit at 11%, not 18%. The 18% figure belongs to on-site caregivers.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Calculate quit-rate drops for caregivers (9 points) and non-caregivers (1 point); contrast is direct.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus:
Vaccine adjuvants are added to stimulate the innate immune cells that help launch an antibody response, and these cells become less responsive with age. Researchers gave younger and older adults a flu vaccine with or without an experimental adjuvant. They measured antibody titers before vaccination and four weeks after. Because baseline titers differ by age, they compared groups using the fold rise: the post-vaccination titer divided by the pre-vaccination titer. They hypothesized that the adjuvant would benefit older adults more than younger adults.

Mean Antibody Titer
Group | Pre-vaccination | Post-vaccination
Younger, standard vaccine | 50 | 400
Younger, with adjuvant | 50 | 500
Older, standard vaccine | 10 | 30
Older, with adjuvant | 10 | 90
choices: The adjuvant raised younger adults' post-vaccination titer by 100, compared with a rise of only 60 for older adults.
The adjuvant raised older adults' fold rise from 3 to 9 but raised younger adults' fold rise only from 8 to 10.
Older adults given the adjuvant reached a titer of 90, three times the 30 reached with the standard vaccine.
Older adults given the adjuvant showed a larger fold rise than younger adults given the same adjuvant did.
explanation: The researchers measure benefit using fold rise, so you have to compute it for all four rows. For older adults, fold rise went from 3 (30 ÷ 10) to 9 (90 ÷ 10). For younger adults, it went from 8 (400 ÷ 50) to 10 (500 ÷ 50). Older adults gained far more, as the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: You used raw titers when the passage said groups are compared by fold rise. The differences of 100 and 60 are accurate. But because baselines differ so much, raw gains don't measure the benefit the researchers defined.

C.why: You stopped at one age group. This choice shows the adjuvant helped older adults, but the hypothesis claims they benefit more than younger adults. That requires the younger adults' data too.

D.why: You misread the adjuvant rows. With the adjuvant, older adults' fold rise was 9 and younger adults' was 10, so older adults' fold rise was not larger. The hypothesis concerns the size of the gain, not the final fold rise.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Requires calculating fold rise ratios for all groups, then interpreting which comparison best shows the hypothesis

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Carvalho's claim?
stimulus:
In a highly reverberant building, each note an organ plays lingers for several seconds, and rapid passages can blur into an indistinct wash. Musicologist Inês Carvalho compared recordings of the same organists performing in acoustically dry churches and in reverberant cathedrals. She reasoned that because blurring is worst when notes follow one another quickly, players would compensate by slowing down. She claimed that reverberation reduces tempo more in fast pieces than in slow ones.

Average Tempo (beats per minute)
Piece type | Dry church | Reverberant cathedral
Fast | 132 | 112
Slow | 64 | 60
choices: Organists slowed fast pieces by 20 beats per minute in reverberant cathedrals but slowed slow pieces by only 4.
Organists played both fast and slow pieces at lower tempos in reverberant cathedrals than in dry churches.
In reverberant cathedrals, organists played fast pieces at 112 beats per minute and slow pieces at 60.
Organists slowed slow pieces by 20 beats per minute in reverberant cathedrals but slowed fast pieces by only 4.
explanation: Carvalho's claim compares the size of the slowdown in the two kinds of piece. Fast pieces dropped from 132 to 112, a fall of 20 beats per minute. Slow pieces dropped from 64 to 60, a fall of 4. Choice A makes that comparison.

B.why: You chose an accurate statement that supports a weaker claim, that reverberation slows tempo in general. Carvalho claims the effect is larger for fast pieces, and this choice doesn't compare the size of the two slowdowns.

C.why: You compared the wrong cells. This choice compares fast and slow pieces within the cathedral column. Fast pieces are faster everywhere, so this says nothing about the effect of reverberation.

D.why: You swapped the rows. Fast pieces lost 20 beats per minute and slow pieces lost 4, not the reverse.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Calculate tempo changes and identify which difference (20 vs 4) supports the claim; distractor D inverts the logic

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken the team's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Adding clay platelets a few nanometers thick to a polymer can stiffen it by restricting how freely its molecular chains slide past one another. This restriction was thought to matter mainly above the polymer's softening point, where the chains move most freely. A materials team tested an epoxy with and without 5% nanoclay at 25°C and at 120°C, a temperature above its softening point. The team hypothesized that nanoclay improves the epoxy's stiffness only at temperatures above that point.

Stiffness (gigapascals)
Test temperature | Without nanoclay | With nanoclay
25°C | 2.4 | 3.1
120°C | 0.6 | 1.4
choices: At 120°C, the epoxy with nanoclay had a stiffness of 1.4 gigapascals, compared with 0.6 without it.
Both versions of the epoxy were stiffer at 25°C than at 120°C, with or without the added nanoclay.
At 25°C, the epoxy with nanoclay had a stiffness of 3.1 gigapascals, compared with 2.4 without it.
At 25°C, the epoxy without nanoclay had a stiffness of 3.1 gigapascals, compared with 2.4 with it.
explanation: The word 'only' is what you need to test. If nanoclay helps only above the softening point, it should make no difference at 25°C. Instead, it raised stiffness from 2.4 to 3.1 gigapascals at 25°C, which undercuts the hypothesis.

A.why: You chose the condition where the hypothesis predicts a benefit. An improvement at 120°C fits the hypothesis, so it can't weaken it. The claim is vulnerable only at the lower temperature.

B.why: You compared the wrong series. This choice compares temperatures within each material. The hypothesis is about the effect of nanoclay at each temperature.

D.why: You swapped the columns. At 25°C, the epoxy with nanoclay measured 3.1 and the one without measured 2.4. The reversed version would actually support the hypothesis.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Must recognize that improvement at 25°C (below softening point) contradicts a hypothesis claiming benefit ONLY above it

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the ecologists' conclusion?
stimulus:
In many songbirds, both parents carry insects to the nest, and a larger brood means more hungry mouths per trip. Ecologists watching blue tit nests counted parents' feeding visits per hour at broods of three and of six chicks. They made counts in a year when caterpillars were plentiful and in a year when a late frost made them scarce. They measured provisioning as visits per chick: hourly visits divided by brood size. They concluded that when food is scarce, chicks in large broods are fed less often than chicks in small broods.

Parental Feeding Visits per Hour
Year | Brood of three | Brood of six
Plentiful caterpillars | 12 | 24
Scarce caterpillars | 12 | 15
choices: In the scarce year, parents of six-chick broods made 15 visits per hour, more than the 12 made by parents of three-chick broods.
In the scarce year, chicks in broods of six received 2.5 visits each per hour, while chicks in broods of three received 4.
In the plentiful year, parents of six-chick broods made 24 visits per hour, twice the 12 made by parents of three-chick broods.
In the plentiful year, chicks in broods of six received fewer visits each per hour than chicks in broods of three did.
explanation: The conclusion applies to the scarce year and depends on visits per chick, so you have to divide. In the scarce year, 15 ÷ 6 = 2.5 visits per chick in large broods and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 in small broods. Chicks in large broods were fed less often, as the ecologists concluded.

A.why: You used raw hourly visits when the ecologists defined provisioning per chick. Large-brood parents made more total visits, but those visits were shared among twice as many chicks.

C.why: You ignored the condition the claim depends on. The conclusion concerns the year when food was scarce, and this choice reports the plentiful year using raw totals instead of visits per chick.

D.why: You misread the plentiful year. Chicks in both brood sizes received 4 visits each per hour (24 ÷ 6 and 12 ÷ 3), so large-brood chicks did not receive fewer.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content
rated_why: Requires dividing visits by brood size to get per-chick rate; distractor A uses raw totals that superficially look larger

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus:
Landmarks Correctly Located (%)
Terrain | Contour lines only | Contour lines + hillshading
Flat plains | 81 | 80
Rolling hills | 74 | 79
Steep mountains | 52 | 77

Topographic maps traditionally show elevation with contour lines, which are precise but require readers to mentally reconstruct the shape of the land. Hillshading, which simulates sunlight falling across slopes, makes relief visible at a glance. Cartographer Inés Valcárcel and colleagues asked participants to locate landmarks on maps of three regions. Each map was drawn in two versions that were identical except that one added hillshading. Because contour lines crowd together and become harder to decode as slopes steepen, the researchers hypothesized that the benefit of hillshading grows as terrain becomes more rugged.
choices: On the steep-mountain maps, participants using contour lines alone correctly located only 52% of the landmarks.
Hillshading improved accuracy for every terrain type, and its largest improvement occurred on the steep-mountain maps.
Hillshading raised accuracy by 25 points on steep-mountain maps and by 5 points on rolling-hill maps, but not on flat-plain maps.
Participants using hillshaded maps were more accurate on flat-plain maps (80%) than on steep-mountain maps (77%).
explanation: The hypothesis is about the benefit of hillshading, which is the gap between the two columns, and it predicts that this gap widens as terrain gets more rugged. Work out the gap for each row: flat plains 80 − 81 = −1 (no benefit), rolling hills 79 − 74 = +5, steep mountains 77 − 52 = +25. The benefit rises steadily from flat to rolling to steep, which is the pattern the researchers predicted.

A.why: The number is accurate, but it comes from one column only. It shows that steep contour maps are hard to read. It doesn't show how much hillshading helps, because a benefit needs a comparison between the two map versions.

B.why: This one is close, because the largest gain really is in the mountains. But hillshading didn't improve accuracy for every terrain type: on flat plains it went from 81% to 80%. Check every part of a choice against the table, not just the part that matches the hypothesis.

D.why: Both numbers are correct, but they come from the same series, the hillshading column, in two terrains. The hypothesis is about the gap between the shaded and unshaded versions, so comparing within one column misses the comparison the claim needs.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
Cyclist Ridership and Injuries by Corridor Type
Corridor type | Period | Daily cyclists | Annual cyclist injuries
Protected lanes | Before | 2,000 | 16
Protected lanes | After | 5,000 | 20
Painted lanes | Before | 2,000 | 14
Painted lanes | After | 2,500 | 20

When a city separates bike lanes from traffic with curbs or planters, ridership on those streets often climbs, so total crash counts can rise even if each trip becomes safer. To isolate risk, transportation analyst Kofi Mensah's team compared corridors that received protected lanes with similar corridors that received only painted lanes. For each corridor they calculated an injury rate: annual cyclist injuries per 1,000 daily cyclists. The team concluded that protected lanes made cycling safer for each rider, even though injuries on those corridors rose in number. Data from the table support this conclusion: ______
choices: on protected-lane corridors, annual injuries rose from 16 to 20, matching the final total recorded on painted-lane corridors.
on protected-lane corridors, the injury rate fell from 8 to 4 per 1,000 daily cyclists but rose from 7 to 8 on painted-lane ones.
on protected-lane corridors, daily cyclists rose from 2,000 to 5,000, a far larger gain than painted-lane corridors experienced.
on painted-lane corridors, the injury rate fell from 8 to 7 per 1,000 daily cyclists, a smaller drop than protected lanes saw.
explanation: The conclusion concerns safety for each rider, so you need the rate the passage defines, not raw counts. Protected lanes: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 before and 20 ÷ 5 = 4 after, so the rate halved. Painted lanes: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 before and 20 ÷ 2.5 = 8 after, so the rate rose. Risk per rider fell only where protected lanes went in, even though injuries there rose from 16 to 20. That is exactly what the team concluded.

A.why: The figures are accurate, but they are raw injury counts. The passage tells you that safety for each rider depends on injuries per 1,000 daily cyclists. Rising raw counts are the 'even though' part of the conclusion, not the evidence that cycling became safer.

C.why: Ridership did rise sharply, but ridership alone says nothing about risk. You need to divide injuries by cyclists to see whether each rider became safer.

D.why: This gets the painted-lane rate backwards. It went from 7 to 8 (14 ÷ 2 to 20 ÷ 2.5), so it rose rather than falling. 8 and 7 are the right numbers in the wrong order, which suggests you mixed up the before and after rows or took 8 from the protected-lane row.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
stimulus:
Many songbirds sing at dawn, when the air is still and sound carries far. Ornithologist Talia Brenner noticed that house wrens nesting along a commuter highway in Ohio seemed to start singing unusually early, possibly to finish before the morning traffic peaks. Traffic on that highway is far lighter on weekends. Brenner therefore reasoned that if traffic, rather than some other feature of roadside habitat, causes the early start, the shift should shrink on weekends. Her data support this hypothesis: ______

Mean Start of Dawn Song (minutes before sunrise)
Nest location | Weekdays | Weekends
Roadside | 52 | 38
Forest interior | 36 | 35
choices: on weekdays, roadside wrens began singing 52 minutes before sunrise, much earlier than forest-interior wrens, which began 36 minutes before.
roadside wrens began singing 52 minutes before sunrise on weekdays but only 38 minutes before on weekends, while forest-interior wrens shifted by just 1 minute.
forest-interior wrens began singing slightly earlier on weekends, at 35 minutes before sunrise, than they did on weekdays, at 36 minutes before.
roadside wrens began singing earlier than forest-interior wrens did on weekends as well as on weekdays, at 38 versus 35 minutes before sunrise.
explanation: Brenner's claim is narrower than 'roadside wrens sing early.' She says traffic causes the early start, so the early start should shrink when traffic drops. To show that, you need the roadside wrens' weekday and weekend times side by side (52 versus 38 minutes), plus a check that interior wrens, which hear no traffic, barely change (36 versus 35). Choice B makes exactly that comparison.

A.why: This is accurate, but it compares the two sites on weekdays only. A weekday gap could come from any difference between roadside and forest habitat, which is the very explanation Brenner wants to rule out. You picked a true sentence that compares the wrong cells.

C.why: The figures are minutes before sunrise, so 36 is earlier than 35. Interior wrens actually started slightly earlier on weekdays. You reversed the direction of the scale.

D.why: The numbers are right, but this choice stresses that roadside wrens stay earlier even on weekends. It never shows the weekday-to-weekend drop the hypothesis predicts. You matched the topic but skipped the condition, light traffic, that the claim depends on.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Okafor's hypothesis?
stimulus:
In many shrublands, rodents eat or store a large share of the seeds that fall to the ground. Ecologist Amaka Okafor suspected that fire alters this pattern. Burning clears the low cover that rodents use to hide from owls and foxes, so it should make them less willing to linger over large seeds, which take a long time to husk. Their harvest of small, quickly eaten seeds should stay largely unchanged. Because the burned plots were smaller, Okafor set out fewer seeds in them.

Seeds Removed by Rodents After 10 Days
Plot type | Seed size | Seeds set out | Seeds removed
Unburned | Large | 400 | 240
Burned | Large | 200 | 60
Unburned | Small | 400 | 100
Burned | Small | 200 | 50
choices: Rodents removed 240 of 400 large seeds from unburned plots but 60 of 200 from burned plots, and one-fourth of the small seeds in each plot type.
Rodents removed 240 large seeds from unburned plots but only 60 from burned plots, and 100 small seeds from unburned plots but only 50 from burned plots.
In burned plots, rodents removed 60 large seeds and 50 small seeds, so they took only slightly more large seeds than small seeds there.
In burned plots, rodents removed a smaller proportion of the large seeds set out than of the small seeds set out in those same plots.
explanation: Burned plots received half as many seeds, so raw counts can't be compared. You have to compare proportions. For large seeds, removal fell from 60% (240 of 400) to 30% (60 of 200). For small seeds it held at 25% in both plot types (100 of 400 and 50 of 200). Fire lowered large-seed removal and left small-seed removal unchanged, which is just what Okafor predicted.

B.why: You used raw counts. Read that way, fire seems to halve small-seed removal too, which would cut against the hypothesis. That drop only exists because half as many seeds were set out in burned plots. As a proportion, small-seed removal didn't change.

C.why: The counts are accurate, but they come from burned plots alone. The hypothesis is about how fire changes removal, so you have to compare burned with unburned plots. Comparing the two seed sizes inside one plot type doesn't test that.

D.why: In burned plots, rodents took 30% of large seeds (60 of 200) and 25% of small seeds (50 of 200). The large-seed proportion was higher, not lower. You likely assumed the hypothesis predicts this without working out the proportions.

license: CC BY 4.0 - original item, not College Board content

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Duarte's hypothesis?
stimulus:
When an athlete's core body temperature climbs toward about 40°C, the brain reduces muscle activation, and the athlete slows or stops. An ice-packed vest worn during a warm-up lowers core temperature before exercise begins, which should lengthen the time an athlete can work before reaching that limit. In mild weather, however, core temperature rarely approaches the limit. Sports scientist Rafael Duarte therefore hypothesized that pre-cooling extends cyclists' time to exhaustion in hot conditions but has little effect in mild ones.

Mean Time to Exhaustion (minutes)
Condition | No vest | Vest
Mild (18°C) | 46 | 47
Hot (34°C) | 27 | 35
choices: Without the vest, cyclists lasted 46 minutes in mild conditions but only 27 minutes in hot conditions, a drop of 19 minutes.
With the vest, cyclists lasted longer than they did without it in both conditions, reaching 47 minutes in mild and 35 in hot conditions.
In hot conditions, the vest raised time to exhaustion from 27 to 35 minutes, while in mild conditions it raised it only from 46 to 47 minutes.
Cyclists who wore the vest in hot conditions lasted nearly as long as cyclists who wore the vest in mild conditions did.
explanation: The hypothesis makes two predictions: the vest helps a lot in heat and barely at all in mild weather. Supporting it means showing the vest's effect under each condition. Choice C does that: 8 extra minutes in heat (27 to 35) and 1 extra minute in mild weather (46 to 47).

A.why: This is accurate, but it compares the two no-vest cells. It shows that heat shortens endurance, not that the vest helps. You read the wrong row-and-column pair.

B.why: This is true, but it leaves out the no-vest values, so you can't tell how big the vest's effect was in each condition. The hypothesis depends on the effect being large in heat and small in mild weather. Saying 'longer in both' ignores the condition the claim turns on.

D.why: Vest-wearers lasted 35 minutes in heat and 47 in mild weather, a 12-minute gap. That isn't 'nearly as long.' You may have assumed the vest cancels out heat completely, which the table doesn't show.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the text?
stimulus:
Performers of Baroque music often slow down at a movement's final cadence, a practice called ritardando. Some critics link a pronounced final ritardando to ensembles that play on period instruments. After measuring the final slowing in 120 recordings, musicologist Hanne Lindqvist concluded that period-instrument ensembles do slow more than modern-instrument ensembles, but that the difference is concentrated in slow movements. As evidence, she points out that ______

Mean Tempo Reduction at Final Cadence (%)
Movement type | Period-instrument ensembles | Modern-instrument ensembles
Fast | 6 | 5
Slow | 14 | 7
choices: period-instrument ensembles slowed by 14% at the final cadences of slow movements but by only 6% at the final cadences of fast movements.
in fast movements, modern-instrument ensembles slowed by a greater percentage at final cadences than period-instrument ensembles did.
period-instrument ensembles slowed by 14% in slow movements, more than double the slowing found in any single modern-instrument recording.
in slow movements, period-instrument ensembles slowed by 14%, twice as much as modern ones, but in fast movements the two differed by 1 point.
explanation: Lindqvist's conclusion compares the two kinds of ensemble and says the gap appears mainly in slow movements. You need the gap in each movement type: 14% versus 7% in slow movements and 6% versus 5% in fast ones. Choice D reports both.

A.why: This compares period ensembles with themselves across movement types. Modern ensembles also slow more in slow movements (7% versus 5%), so this pattern says nothing about a difference between ensembles. You compared the wrong pair of cells.

B.why: In fast movements, period ensembles slowed by 6% and modern ones by 5%. This choice reverses that comparison.

C.why: The table gives averages. It can't tell you how much any single modern recording slowed, and some may have slowed by more than 7%. You treated a mean as if it held for every recording.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ferreira's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Folklorists have long noted that children who hear a familiar tale often object if a teller strays from the expected wording. Such demands for exact repetition could help preserve traditional opening formulas, such as 'Once there was and once there was not.' Where printed collections of local tales circulate, though, tellers can consult a fixed text whatever their audience. Folklorist Nadia Ferreira therefore hypothesizes that tellings for children preserve opening formulas better than tellings for adults do, mainly in communities without printed collections.

Tellings That Kept the Traditional Opening Formula (%)
Community | Told to children | Told to adults
With printed collections | 81 | 77
Without printed collections | 88 | 52
choices: Tellings for adults kept the formula far more often in communities with printed collections, at 77%, than in communities without them, at 52%.
In communities without printed collections, children retelling the tales themselves kept the opening formula in 88% of their own tellings.
Without printed collections, 88% of tellings for children but only 52% for adults kept the formula; with them, the figures were 81% and 77%.
Tellings for children kept the formula more often than tellings for adults did in both kinds of communities, at 81% and 88%, respectively.
explanation: Ferreira's claim has two parts: children's tellings keep the formula better, and that advantage shows up mainly where there are no printed collections. You need the child-versus-adult gap in both kinds of community. Choice C gives it: 36 points without print (88 versus 52) and 4 points with print (81 versus 77).

A.why: This is accurate, but it compares adult tellings across communities. That shows print's effect, not the effect of a child audience. You compared the wrong series.

B.why: The table counts tellings told to children, not tellings by children. You assigned the data to the wrong group.

D.why: This is accurate, but it ignores the word 'mainly' in the hypothesis. Children's tellings lead in both communities, yet only the gap without print is large. Since this choice leaves out the adult values, it can't show where the difference is concentrated.

subtype_name: Use a multi-variable graph or table to support or weaken a researcher's claim
